prompt: Some schools teach children of all abilities together in the same class, while others divide students into groups according to how well they perform. Discuss both approaches and give your own opinion.
essay:
Schools have to decide whether to teach children of different attainment levels together or to separate them into ability groups. Advocates of mixed classes stress fairness and mutual learning; supporters of setting argue that teaching is more effective when a class is at a similar stage. I think setting works for a minority of subjects and does more harm than good elsewhere.

The argument for teaching everyone together is partly moral and partly practical. A child placed in a bottom set at eleven tends to interpret the placement as a permanent statement about their intelligence, and lowered expectations reliably produce lowered results. There is also the difficulty that early attainment often reflects home circumstances rather than capacity, so sorting children young risks converting an accident of background into a fixed educational path.

The case for setting is harder to dismiss than its critics allow. A teacher facing a class with a four-year spread of attainment must either pitch the lesson somewhere in the middle, losing both ends, or prepare three lessons simultaneously. In subjects that build strictly on prior knowledge — mathematics above all — a student who has not mastered the previous stage genuinely cannot access the next one, and pretending otherwise helps nobody. Placing that student in a group working at their actual level is the only arrangement in which they ever catch up.

My own conclusion follows from that distinction. Where a subject is cumulative, grouping by current attainment is a practical necessity rather than a judgement about worth. Where it is not — in history, literature or the arts — a mixed class costs the stronger students little and gives the weaker ones access to better conversation. What matters most is that any grouping remains genuinely temporary and is reviewed often.
title: Mixed-ability classes or setting by ability
